artiest/crosby-stills-nash-en-young.text:
Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young was a group of four songwriters from well-known bands. David Crosby had been fired from The Byrds in late 1967, Stephen Stills came from Buffalo Springfield and Graham Nash from the British band The Hollies. At a party in Laurel Canyon in Los Angeles in 1968, the three discovered how good their voices sounded together. In 1969 Neil Young joined them, like Stills a former member of Buffalo Springfield. The group stands for Californian folk rock and for close harmony: singing in which the voices lie very close together.

The debut Crosby, Stills & Nash (1969) produced Suite: Judy Blue Eyes and Marrakesh Express. With Young, the group played the Woodstock festival in August 1969, according to Stills only their second time in front of an audience. Déjà Vu (March 1970) reached number 1 in America and became their best-selling album. It includes Our House, which Nash wrote in Joni Mitchell's house in Laurel Canyon, where the two lived together. Mitchell's Woodstock is on it too, in a hard-driving rock version. After the shootings at Kent State University in May 1970, in which the National Guard killed four students, Young wrote Ohio.

The 1970 tour, captured on the live album 4 Way Street (1971), was overshadowed by quarrels, and the group broke up soon afterwards. Crosby, Stills & Nash were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997; Young is inducted separately, as a solo artist and with Buffalo Springfield. Crosby died in 2023. With Ohio and Woodstock, the group gave a voice to the protest and counterculture of around 1970.
artiest/crosby-stills-nash-en-young.listen: Listen to Our House (1970) and notice the harmony singing in the chorus. Nash sings the melody, while Crosby and Stills place their voices right alongside it. Underneath, Nash himself plays piano and harpsichord.

artiest/csr-symphony-orchestra-bratislav.text:
The Slovak Radio Symphony Orchestra, in Slovak Symfonický orchester Slovenského rozhlasu, is a radio orchestra from Bratislava. It was previously called the Czecho-Slovak Radio Symphony Orchestra and the CSR Symphony Orchestra. The orchestra was founded in 1929 to provide music for Slovak radio. As a result, it developed a special bond with Slovak composers, in particular Alexander Moyzes, Eugen Suchoň and Ján Cikker.

The first principal conductor was František Dyk. Among those who later stood in front of the orchestra were Krešimir Baranović, Ľudovít Rajter, Ladislav Slovák, Václav Jiráček, Otakar Trhlík and Bystrík Režucha. Ondrej Lenárd led it from 1977 to 1990 and Róbert Stankovský from 1990 to 2001. Later principal conductors included Charles Olivieri-Munroe, Oliver von Dohnányi, Mario Košik and Peter Valentovič. In 2019 Lenárd returned as principal conductor.

Abroad, the orchestra became known through its broadcasts and recordings, especially for the label Naxos Records. It is thus an example of an orchestra that, through radio and inexpensive CDs of classical music, could be heard far beyond its own country. On those recordings it plays both the well-known symphonic repertoire and works by Eastern European composers.
artiest/csr-symphony-orchestra-bratislav.listen: Listen to a recording of the orchestra on the Naxos label and notice the sound of the ensemble as a whole. Can you hear which section of the orchestra, strings or winds, carries the melody?

artiest/cuby-blizzards.text:
Cuby + Blizzards was a blues rock band from the village of Grolloo in Drenthe, which at the time was still spelled Grollo. Singer Harry Muskee and guitarist Eelco Gelling founded the group in 1964. The name came from Muskee's dog Cuby. The band rehearsed in the little farmhouse that Muskee rented in Grolloo, and sounded unlike any other Dutch group of the time: not cheerful beat, but heavy blues with rock 'n' roll running through it.

The first single, Stumble and Fall, appeared in 1965. The debut album Desolation (1966) won an Edison, and Groeten uit Grollo (1967) followed, along with hits such as Another Day, Another Road, Distant Smile and Window of My Eyes. Appleknockers Flophouse came out in 1969. From early 1967 to mid-1969 Herman Brood was at the piano, which launched his own career. The band toured with Van Morrison, made a record with the American bluesman Eddie Boyd and played with Alexis Korner, who can be heard on Live in Düsseldorf (1968). John Mayall even stayed at the farm in Grolloo.

Muskee sang in English with an audibly Dutch accent, and that is precisely what gave the music its own character. In the mid-1970s Gelling left for Golden Earring. From 1996 the band played again, with Erwin Java on guitar, and in 2009 Cats Lost appeared. With the death of Harry Muskee in 2011, Cuby + Blizzards came to a definitive end, the band that gave the blues a home in the Netherlands.
artiest/cuby-blizzards.listen: Listen to Appleknockers Flophouse and notice Harry Muskee's raw voice and Eelco Gelling's guitar playing. Hear how close this band from Drenthe comes to the British and American blues of the time.

artiest/culture-beat.text:
Culture Beat was a German Eurodance project that began in 1989 in Frankfurt. Its creator was Torsten Fenslau, who had actually wanted to become an architect but had been a DJ at the club Dorian Gray since 1982. Together with Jens Zimmermann and Peter Zweier he first made Der Erdbeermund, a club track with spoken German lyrics. He then brought in the American rapper Jay Supreme and the singer Lana Earl. With No Deeper Meaning, from the album Horizon (1991), the group had a sizeable hit in the Netherlands.

The real breakthrough came in 1993. The British singer Tania Evans replaced Lana Earl, and the sound became harder. Mr. Vain reached number 1 in a series of European countries, including Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The album Serenity also produced Got to Get It and Anything. The recipe was typical of the Eurodance of those years: a fast, pounding beat, bright synthesizer parts, a female singer for the chorus and a rapper for the verses. Still in 1993, Fenslau was killed in a car accident at the age of 29. His brother Frank took over the project.

Without Fenslau, Inside Out appeared in 1995, the last album with Evans and Jay Supreme. After that, Culture Beat opted for straightforward pop, with changing female singers, but the great success did not return. Mr. Vain remained one of the songs that sum up the 1990s: a studio product from a German club that conquered all of Europe via radio and dance floor.
artiest/culture-beat.listen: Listen to Mr. Vain and notice the division of labour: the rapper tells the story in the verses, the singer sings the chorus. Hear how the synthesizers and the relentless beat drive the song forward.

artiest/culture-club.text:
Culture Club is an English pop group from London, formed in 1981. Singer Boy George, a regular at the Blitz Club, started his own band with bassist Mikey Craig after a short spell in Bow Wow Wow. Drummer Jon Moss and guitarist and keyboard player Roy Hay completed the group. The name refers to the members' different backgrounds: a gay singer of Irish descent, a black Briton, a blond Englishman and a Jewish drummer.

After two failed singles, the group broke through in 1982 with Do You Really Want to Hurt Me, a song with reggae influences that reached number 1 in many countries. The debut album Kissing to Be Clever also produced Time (Clock of the Heart) and I'll Tumble 4 Ya. The second album, Colour by Numbers from 1983, included Church of the Poison Mind, Miss Me Blind and Karma Chameleon, the band's biggest hit. The music combined new wave with American soul and pop, with touches of reggae, calypso and salsa, and in Karma Chameleon even country.

Culture Club belonged to the New Romantics, and Boy George's striking appearance attracted enormous attention. Thanks to their videos on MTV, the group also became big in America, as part of a new British Invasion. Around 1986 the band broke up, partly because of Boy George's addiction and his relationship with Moss. Reunions followed later.
artiest/culture-club.listen: Listen to Karma Chameleon by Culture Club. Notice the harmonica and the cheerful, almost country-like melody, combined with a supple pop beat.

artiest/curly-russell.text:
Dillon Curley Russell was born in 1917 in Trinidad and died in 1986 in New York. He was an American jazz bassist who can be heard on many bebop recordings. He got his nickname Curley because of his curly hair. He played in the Tadd Dameron Sextet. He was in demand because he could keep up with the breakneck tempos of bebop, and he appears on several key recordings from that period. At the end of the 1950s he left the music world.

On 1 May 1951 he took part in the recording session of Un Poco Loco, a composition by the pianist Bud Powell, with Max Roach on drums. The literary critic Harold Bloom put this piece on his short list of the greatest works of twentieth-century American art.

According to the jazz historian Phil Schaap, the well-known bebop tune Donna Lee is named after Russell's daughter. That tune is a contrafact of Back Home Again in Indiana, that is, a new melody over the chords of an existing song. In 2002 his daughter donated his bass to the Institute of Jazz Studies at Rutgers University. Russell is an example of the bassists who made the bebop sound possible: they held the fast pulse so firmly that the soloists were free to play over the chords.
artiest/curly-russell.listen: Listen to Un Poco Loco by Bud Powell and notice the bass lines beneath the piano and the drums. Can you hear how the bass keeps a steady pulse while everyone else plays busily on?

artiest/curtis-fuller.text:
Curtis Fuller was an American jazz trombonist, born in 1932 in Detroit. His father came from Jamaica and died before he was born; his mother died when he was nine. For a time he grew up in an orphanage. One of the nuns took him to a concert by Illinois Jacquet, with J.J. Johnson on trombone, and there he fell under the spell of jazz. At sixteen he began to play the trombone. At school he was in the same class as future jazz musicians such as Paul Chambers, Donald Byrd and Tommy Flanagan.

In the army he played in a band with Chambers and the brothers Cannonball and Nat Adderley. He then played with Yusef Lateef, with whom he went to New York in 1957. There he made his first records as a bandleader for Prestige. Alfred Lion of Blue Note brought him to his label and put him on recordings by Sonny Clark and by John Coltrane, on the 1957 album Blue Train. Later he played with Bud Powell, Jimmy Smith, Wayne Shorter, Lee Morgan and Joe Henderson.

Fuller was the first trombonist in the Jazztet of Art Farmer and Benny Golson, and from 1961 to 1965 he played in Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. He played hard bop, a robust, swinging form of jazz with long solos, and showed that the trombone could be just as agile in it as a saxophone. In 2007 he was honoured as an NEA Jazz Master. He died in 2021.
artiest/curtis-fuller.listen: Listen to Blue Train by John Coltrane. Notice Curtis Fuller's solo after those of Coltrane and Lee Morgan: hear how he plays warm, rounded lines on the trombone above the swinging rhythm section.

artiest/curtis-mayfield.text: Curtis Mayfield was born in Chicago in 1942. He was the singer, guitarist and songwriter of the soul group The Impressions and in 1968 founded his own record label, Curtom. His music for Super Fly (1972) was a huge success. The album topped the American chart, and Freddie's Dead and Superfly each sold more than a million copies. The lyrics do not glorify the drug life but warn against it. He then wrote and produced soundtracks for other singers: Claudine (1974) with Gladys Knight & the Pips, Let's Do It Again (1975) with the Staple Singers and Sparkle (1976) with Aretha Franklin. In 1990 he was paralysed in an accident on stage.
artiest/curtis-mayfield.listen: Notice the funky guitar, the strings and horns above it and Mayfield's high falsetto voice, which uses the lyrics to comment on what is happening on screen.

artiest/cybotron.text:
Cybotron was an electronic duo from Detroit, formed around 1980 by Juan Atkins and Richard Davis, who also called himself 3070. Detroit was then a city in decline: the car industry was shrinking and many neighbourhoods were emptying out. In that setting, Atkins and Davis made music about machines, cities and the future. They released their first records, Alleys of Your Mind and Cosmic Cars, on Atkins's own label, Deep Space Records. The influential Detroit radio DJ The Electrifying Mojo played them, and so the group quickly became known.

In 1983 the album Enter appeared, featuring Clear and Techno City. Cybotron blended the funk of George Clinton with the electronic music of Kraftwerk and Yellow Magic Orchestra. Drum machines and synthesizers were not an aid but the heart of the music. The rhythms are repetitive and mechanical, the melodies synthetic. Books such as Alvin Toffler's Future Shock also inspired the duo, and their image of black musicians in a technological future is often counted as part of Afrofuturism.

After a disagreement with Davis, Atkins left in the mid-1980s. Davis continued under the name Cybotron, while Atkins, as Model 500 and with his label Metroplex, shaped the sound of Detroit techno. That puts Cybotron at the beginning of techno, which crossed over to the United Kingdom in the late 1980s and fed rave culture there. Clear has often been sampled since.
artiest/cybotron.listen: Listen to Clear and notice the drum machine and the repeated synthesizer patterns. Hear how the track sounds funky and danceable almost without any ordinary instruments.

artiest/cyndi-lauper.text:
Cyndi Lauper was born in 1953 in Brooklyn, New York, and grew up in Ozone Park in Queens. As a child she listened to the Beatles and Judy Garland. At twelve she began writing songs on an acoustic guitar she was given by her sister. In 1978 she formed the band Blue Angel with the saxophonist John Turi. Their only album, Blue Angel from 1980, sold poorly and the group split up. After that she was penniless and sang in local clubs, until she got a contract with Portrait Records in 1981.

Her solo debut She's So Unusual appeared in 1983 and became a worldwide hit. It was the first debut album by a woman to produce four top-five hits on the American Hot 100: Girls Just Want to Have Fun, Time After Time, She Bop and All Through the Night. Lauper co-wrote some of the songs herself, including Time After Time and She Bop. She rewrote the lyrics of Girls Just Want to Have Fun into a song for young women. In 1985 she won a Grammy for Best New Artist. She also sang on We Are the World. The second album, True Colors from 1986, yielded two more top-five hits.

Her colourful hair and clothes were striking, as was her voice with a range of four octaves. Later she made Memphis Blues in 2010, which spent thirteen weeks at the top of the Billboard blues albums chart. In 2013 she won a Tony for the music of the musical Kinky Boots, the first woman to win that award on her own. She also campaigns for LGBTQ rights. In November 2025 she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/cyndi-lauper.listen: Listen to Time After Time and notice how her voice moves from soft to full in the chorus. Can you hear the long breath with which she carries the melody?

artiest/cynthia-weil.text:
Cynthia Weil was an American lyricist, born in 1940 in New York. She grew up in Manhattan in a Jewish family and trained as an actress and dancer. It soon became clear that she was good at writing songs. Around 1960 she joined Don Kirshner's music publisher Aldon Music, and so became one of the writers associated with the Brill Building in New York. There she met the composer Barry Mann, whom she married in 1961.

Mann usually wrote the music and Weil the lyrics. Together they created great ballads such as On Broadway and You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin', and hard-hitting rock songs such as Kicks and We Gotta Get Out of This Place. Weil liked to write lyrics with substance. Uptown is about the gap between rich and poor, On Broadway about how hard it is to make it in the big city, and Only in America was about segregation and racism. We Gotta Get Out of This Place became an anthem for soldiers in Vietnam and for young people who wanted to get away.

Weil and Mann thus belonged to the songwriting duos who defined the sound of pop in the 1960s, alongside Carole King and Gerry Goffin, among others. Later they also wrote for films, and for Somewhere Out There Weil received two Grammys. The couple were inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1987 and into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2010. Weil died in 2023.
artiest/cynthia-weil.listen: Listen to You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' by The Righteous Brothers. Notice how Weil's lyrics tell the story of a love slipping away and how the music builds towards a big, dramatic chorus.

artiest/cyrus-chestnut.text:
Cyrus Chestnut is an American jazz pianist, composer and producer, born in 1963 in Baltimore. His father was a postman and church pianist; his mother worked for social services and led a church choir. Chestnut began piano lessons at seven and played as a child in the Mount Calvary Baptist Church. At nine he studied classical music at the Peabody Institute. In 1985 he graduated in jazz composition and arranging from the Berklee College of Music in Boston. The church, classical music and jazz all three belong to his playing.

In the late 1980s and early 1990s he worked with Wynton Marsalis, Terence Blanchard and Donald Harrison. In the early 1990s he joined the band of the singer Betty Carter and played on her 1992 album It's Not About the Melody. That same year he recorded his first albums as a bandleader, The Nutman Speaks and Nut. Later records include Revelation in 1994, Earth Stories in 1996, Soul Food in 2001, Cyrus Plays Elvis in 2007 and Soul Brother Cool in 2013.

On Genuine Chestnut from 2006 he plays with his regular trio and gives jazz versions of well-known pop songs, such as If by Bread. His own Mason Dixon Line on the album is a cheerful bebop number. Time magazine called him the best jazz pianist of his generation in 2006, because he dares to leave notes out and to play space. Chestnut is thus an example of a pianist who combines jazz, gospel and pop in a natural way.
artiest/cyrus-chestnut.listen: Listen to his version of If on Genuine Chestnut and notice the silences between the notes. Can you hear how he gives the familiar pop song room to breathe?

artiest/d-angelo.text:
D'Angelo's real name was Michael Eugene Archer, and he was born in 1974 in Richmond, Virginia. His father was a minister in a Pentecostal church, and as a child he played piano in church. With his group Precise he won Amateur Night at the Apollo Theater in Harlem three times in a row in 1991. He then moved to New York. His first success came in 1994 with U Will Know, a song he wrote and produced for the R&B supergroup Black Men United.

His debut album Brown Sugar appeared in 1995. D'Angelo played many of the instruments himself and drew on the soul of the 1970s, with warm keyboards, slow grooves and layered vocals. Critics see the album as the beginning of neo-soul. He collaborated with Erykah Badu and sang the duet Nothing Even Matters (1998) with Lauryn Hill. In 2000 came Voodoo, a looser and rawer album that entered at the top of the Billboard 200 and won a Grammy. The video for Untitled (How Does It Feel) made him a sex symbol against his will.

After that, D'Angelo withdrew. He struggled with depression and addiction, and only in 2014 did his third and last album appear, Black Messiah, which was again awarded a Grammy. He died in 2025 of pancreatic cancer, while working on a fourth album. With only three albums he became one of the most important names in R&B around the turn of the century.
artiest/d-angelo.listen: Listen to Brown Sugar and notice the slow, languid groove and the warm keyboard sounds. Hear how D'Angelo layers his voice on top of itself, as in the soul of the 1970s.

artiest/d-mob.text:
D Mob is the name under which Daniel Kojo Poku performed, a British producer and remixer born in 1963. He also used the names Dancin' Danny D and Danny D. In 1988 D Mob had a hit with We Call It Acieed, one of the singles that made acid house popular during the Second Summer of Love. The song reached number three in the British chart. The director Marek Budzynski made the video.

In 1989 and 1990 three more British top-twenty singles followed: It Is Time to Get Funky, C'mon and Get My Love and Put Your Hands Together. The album A Little Bit of This, a Little Bit of That appeared in 1989. C'mon and Get My Love, sung by Cathy Dennis, reached number ten on the American Billboard Hot 100 in 1990 and so also found its way onto pop radio. On the American dance club chart, four songs reached number one, including We Call It Acieed and That's the Way of the World.

Dancin' Danny D also worked with Dannii Minogue and later became active as a publisher and manager. Together with Tim Blacksmith he founded the publishing company Stellar Songs, and they managed the Norwegian production team Stargate. In 2022 both men received an MBE for services to music. D Mob shows how acid house found its way from the underground into the charts.
artiest/d-mob.listen: Listen to We Call It Acieed and notice the repeating electronic bass line and the rhythm. Can you hear how little it takes to get you dancing?

artiest/daddy-yankee.text:
Daddy Yankee is the stage name of Ramón Luis Ayala Rodríguez, a Puerto Rican rapper, singer and songwriter, born in 1976. He first wanted to become a professional baseball player, but chose music after a shooting incident. In 1995 he independently released his debut album No Mercy. The follow-up El cangri.com from 2002 was successful in the United States. He is called the King of Reggaeton and is often cited as an example by other Spanish-language urban artists.

The breakthrough came with Barrio fino in 2004, the best-selling Latin album of the 2000s. Its best-known single, Gasolina, was nominated for a Latin Grammy and is seen as the song that introduced reggaeton to a worldwide audience. El cartel: The Big Boss from 2007 reached the top ten of the Billboard 200. In 2017 he made Despacito with Luis Fonsi, the first Spanish-language song since Macarena in 1996 to top the American Hot 100. The accompanying video was for years the most-watched on YouTube.

In 2022 he announced his retirement, which took effect in December 2023 with a final performance in Puerto Rico. In 2025 he returned with Lamento and Baile. Among other honours he won five Latin Grammys and appeared in the Time 100 in 2006. Reggaeton combines rap and singing over a recognizable dembow rhythm, with Caribbean influences. Daddy Yankee turned that style into a worldwide phenomenon.
artiest/daddy-yankee.listen: Listen to Gasolina and notice the hard, constantly recurring rhythm beneath the rap. Try to hear how the chorus is built almost like a shout.

artiest/daf.text:
DAF, in full Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft, was a German band from Düsseldorf, formed in 1978. Singer Gabi Delgado-López and drummer Robert Görl met at the punk club Ratinger Hof. In the first years more musicians played with them, on guitar, bass and electronics. The first album, from 1979, consisted of improvised instrumental pieces. The band then moved to London, where Daniel Miller signed them to his label Mute.

From 1981 DAF consisted of only Delgado and Görl. At Virgin, with the producer Conny Plank, they made three albums: Alles ist gut, Gold und Liebe and Für immer. The sound was stark and hard. Görl played simple, tight drum patterns, and an analogue synthesizer, driven by a sequencer, kept repeating a single line that was both melody and bass line. Over it, Delgado sang or shouted short German phrases. Der Mussolini became a hit, and DAF became a pop group in Germany and was praised by critics in England. During the recording of Für immer the duo broke up.

The band belonged to the Neue Deutsche Welle, but its influence reached much further. The members themselves called their music electronic body music, and DAF is regarded as one of the first electronic body music bands. House and techno also drew on their approach. The radio DJ John Peel even called them the grandfathers of techno. Reunions followed later. Delgado-López died in 2020.
artiest/daf.listen: Listen to Der Mussolini by DAF. Notice the single synthesizer line that runs through the whole song and is bass and melody at once, the tight drums underneath, and Gabi Delgado's short, shouted phrases.

artiest/daft-punk.text: Daft Punk was a French duo of Thomas Bangalter (1975) and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo (1974), formed in 1993 in Paris. With albums such as Homework (1997) and Discovery (2001) they helped to make French house big. Their work with film began with Interstella 5555 (2003), an animated film set to the music of Discovery. In 2006 they directed the experimental film Electroma themselves. For Tron: Legacy (2010) they wrote a full film score. It was recorded with an 85-piece orchestra at AIR Lyndhurst in London. Joseph Trapanese orchestrated and worked with the duo for two years. Synthesizer arpeggios and strings are closely interwoven in it. In the film they appear themselves, with their helmets, in the club End of Line. In 2021 the duo stopped.
artiest/daft-punk.listen: Notice how synthesizer arpeggios and strings play the same rhythmic figures and alternate with one another, and how the orchestra takes over the role of a pad synthesizer.

artiest/daler-mehndi.text:
Daler Mehndi, born Daler Singh in 1967 in Patna, Bihar, comes from a Punjabi Sikh family. In 1991 he formed a group with his brothers, cousins and friends. In 1994 he won the Voice of Asia competition in Almaty, Kazakhstan. He helped make bhangra known worldwide, and Indian pop music independent of the Bollywood film. His trademarks are dance numbers, a turban and long flowing robes.

He signed a three-album contract with Magnasound. His debut Bolo Ta Ra Ra sold more than twenty million copies and made him a pop star. The follow-up Dardi Rab Rab did even better, and in 1997 came Balle Balle, which won six Channel V Awards. That year he also sang the song Na Na Na Re for the Bollywood film Mrityudata, in which he appeared on screen with Amitabh Bachchan. In 1998 Tunak Tunak Tun appeared, with a video with what was then an unprecedented budget of 25 million rupees. The song was a great success in India and later became known internationally too. The album won the Screen Award for best Indian pop album in 1998.

The music combines the driving rhythms and the singing of Punjabi bhangra with pop production. In 2014 Mehndi made an electronic remix of Tunak Tunak Tun together with Deadmau5, a sign that his song found a second life far beyond India. He has performed in dozens of countries, including the Netherlands.
artiest/daler-mehndi.listen: Listen to Tunak Tunak Tun and notice the compelling, repeated rhythm patterns and Mehndi's powerful voice. How does the song keep the energy high without the melody becoming complicated?

artiest/damon-albarn.text:
Damon Albarn is an English musician, born in 1968 in London. His father was an artist and his mother a set designer, and at home they played blues, Indian ragas and African music. He learned guitar, piano and violin and wrote compositions at a young age. At school in Essex he met Graham Coxon. After a brief spell at drama school he went to study music at Goldsmiths College in London. There, in 1988, Albarn, Coxon, bassist Alex James and drummer Dave Rowntree formed a band that was named Blur in 1990.

After the debut Leisure in 1991 and long tours of America, Albarn drew more and more inspiration from British bands of the 1960s. This gave rise to Modern Life Is Rubbish, Parklife and The Great Escape. Blur became one of the big names of Britpop, with a famous rivalry with Oasis. After that the sound changed: on Blur, 13 and Think Tank, lo-fi, art rock, electronica and world music were added.

In 1998 Albarn started the virtual band Gorillaz with the comic artist Jamie Hewlett, with cartoon band members and music full of hip hop, electronica and world music. He also worked with musicians from Mali, founded Africa Express, played in The Good, the Bad & the Queen and wrote music for opera and theatre. As a solo artist he made, among other things, Everyday Robots. He is regarded as one of the most influential British musicians of his generation, precisely because he keeps trying something new.
artiest/damon-albarn.listen: Listen to Parklife by Blur. Notice the ironic, half-spoken verses and the singalong chorus: here Albarn plays with typically English imagery and humour.

artiest/dan-wilson.text:
Dan Wilson is an American musician, songwriter and producer, born in 1961 and raised in St. Louis Park, Minnesota. He studied visual art at Harvard and afterwards first worked as a draughtsman and painter. While still a student he was already making music with his brother Matt. In 1987 he joined Trip Shakespeare, his brother's psychedelic pop rock band in Minneapolis.

After the end of that band he formed the group Semisonic in 1992 with bassist John Munson and drummer Jacob Slichter. Their 1998 album Feeling Strangely Fine brought the breakthrough, with the song Closing Time, which Wilson wrote. It became one of the best-known rock songs of the late 1990s. Secret Smile was also an international hit. Semisonic made clear, melodic guitar pop.

After that Wilson became best known as a writer for others. He wrote Not Ready to Make Nice with The Chicks and Someone Like You with Adele. For Adele's album 21 he received a Grammy. He also worked with Taylor Swift, Chris Stapleton, Jon Batiste and many others, and made solo albums such as Free Life, produced by Rick Rubin. He has been called the songwriter's songwriter: someone who helps others pour their own story into a strong song.
artiest/dan-wilson.listen: Listen to Someone Like You by Adele. Notice the simple, constantly repeated piano accompaniment and how the melody rises in the chorus and lets the emotion grow.

artiest/dandy-livingstone.text:
Dandy Livingstone, born Robert Livingstone Thompson in 1943, is a British-Jamaican musician and producer of ska, rocksteady and reggae. At fifteen he moved from Jamaica to London to live with his mother. His first record came out without his knowledge: a tenant in the building recorded a number of jam sessions and released them on the label Planetone. Carnival Records then went looking for a Jamaican vocal duo. Livingstone recorded both voices himself, under the name Sugar & Dandy. The single What a Life sold 25,000 copies. In the early 1960s he made some of the best-selling British ska singles.

In 1967 he signed with Ska Beat Records, where his debut album Rocksteady with Dandy appeared. A year later he moved into production and formed a duo with Audrey Hall. Among other things he produced Suzanne Beware of the Devil by Nicky Thomas and Red Red Wine by Tony Tribe. At Trojan Records he released Dandy Returns, and in 1972 he had a hit of his own with Suzanne Beware of the Devil, which reached number fourteen in the British chart.

His best-known song of his own is Rudy, a Message to You, on which the trombonist Rico Rodriguez played. The Specials turned it into a hit in 1979. Livingstone also produced singles by Rodriguez under the name Rico & the Rudies. In this way he formed a link between Jamaican music and the British second generation, which later breathed new life into ska.
artiest/dandy-livingstone.listen: Listen to Rudy, a Message to You, first in the version by the Specials and then in the original. What stays the same and what has changed?

artiest/daniel-lohues.text:
Daniël Lohues was born in 1971 in Emmen and grew up in Erica, in Drenthe. His father was an organist and taught him as a child to play the church organ. At thirteen he got his first guitar and started a band. In 1994 he founded Skik, a group that sang in the Drents dialect and had hits in the 1990s with Op fietse, Hoe kan dat nou? and 't Giet zoas 't giet. Skik played at Pinkpop and Lowlands in 1997 and 1998.

In 2003 Lohues started a new band, Lohues & the Louisiana Blues Club, after recording an album in the United States with local blues musicians. A documentary about that adventure premiered at the Netherlands Film Festival, and in 2007 the band opened for The Rolling Stones. He then went solo with theatre tours such as Allennig and released an album nearly every spring. Hier kom ik weg, in 2008 the B-side of the single Baat bij muziek, grew into one of his most popular songs and has been in the Top 2000 since 2009. The album Hout moet received an Edison in 2011, and D from 2014 entered at number 1 in the Album Top 100.

Since 2002 Lohues has also written a weekly column, and he has written songs for, among others, Guus Meeuwis, Freek de Jonge and Paul de Leeuw. He is one of the best-known dialect singers in the Netherlands and contributed to the fame of the Drents dialect beyond Drenthe. In 2020 he received the Culturele prijs van Drenthe, the province's cultural prize.
artiest/daniel-lohues.listen: Listen to Hier kom ik weg and notice how calm the lyrics sound, sung in the Drents dialect. What atmosphere do the voice and the simple accompaniment create?

artiest/daniel-lopatin.text:
Daniel Lopatin was born in 1982 in Massachusetts, the son of Russian-Jewish emigrants with a musical background. He attributes a large part of his taste to his father's record collection and to his father's Roland Juno-60 synthesizer, which he later inherited and used extensively. He studied archival science at the Pratt Institute in Brooklyn and ended up in the noise scene there. Under the name Oneohtrix Point Never, OPN for short, he made electronic music. The name is a play on words on a radio station in Boston.

His first records drew inspiration from arpeggio synthesizer music of the 1970s and 1980s, new age and noise. The compilation Rifts from 2009 earned him critical praise. In 2010 came, as a side project, Chuck Person's Eccojams Vol. 1, which influenced vaporwave. In 2013 he signed with Warp Records. Albums followed such as Age Of in 2018, Magic Oneohtrix Point Never in 2020, Again in 2023 and Tranquilizer in 2025. His music gathers sounds from all kinds of eras and styles, from advertising jingles to minimalism and noise.

Lopatin also made film music, mainly with the Safdie brothers, for Good Time in 2017, Uncut Gems in 2019 and Marty Supreme in 2025. For Good Time he won the Soundtrack Award at the Cannes film festival. He also produced for, among others, The Weeknd, on After Hours, Dawn FM and Hurry Up Tomorrow, whose film music he also co-composed.
artiest/daniel-lopatin.listen: Listen to an excerpt from the music of Uncut Gems and notice the layers of synthesizer. Can you hear how the sound builds tension without there being a clear song?

artiest/dannie-richmond.text:
Charles Daniel Richmond, known as Dannie Richmond, was an American jazz drummer, best known for his work with Charles Mingus. He was born in 1931 in New York and grew up in Greensboro, North Carolina. His first instrument was the tenor saxophone, which he began playing at thirteen. In 1955 he played rhythm and blues in Paul Williams's band. His career changed when he switched to the drums, an instrument he had taught himself in his early twenties.

That led to a twenty-one-year collaboration with Charles Mingus. The biographer Brian Priestley writes that Richmond was to Mingus what Harry Carney was to Ellington's band: an indispensable ingredient of the Mingus sound and also a good friend. Richmond also played with Joe Cocker, Elton John and Mark-Almond. After Mingus's death he became, in 1980, the first musical director of Mingus Dynasty.

His own records included In Jazz for the Culture Set in 1965, Ode to Mingus in 1979, Hand to Hand in 1980 and Plays Charles Mingus in 1981. He died in 1988 in Harlem of a heart attack. Anyone who wants to understand the sound of Mingus has to listen to Richmond: his playing put its stamp on the rough, passionate way that band sounded. He is thus one of the best examples of a drummer who helps shape a bandleader's sound.
artiest/dannie-richmond.listen: Listen to a recording of Mingus with Richmond and notice the drums. Can you hear how the drummer moves with the changing mood of the band?

artiest/danny-cedrone.text:
Donato Joseph Danny Cedrone was born in 1920 in Jamesville, New York State, and died in 1954. He was an American guitarist and bandleader, best known for his work with Bill Haley & His Comets on Rock Around the Clock. His career began in the 1940s, but he only really came into his own in the early 1950s, as a session guitarist for the country group Bill Haley and His Saddlemen from Chester, Pennsylvania. In 1951 he played lead guitar on their recording of Rocket 88, one of the first recognized rock and roll recordings.

Cedrone also formed his own group, the Esquire Boys. That is probably one of the reasons he never became a permanent member of Haley's group. In 1952 he played lead guitar on Rock the Joint. His fast solo, with a jazzy first half and a lightning-fast descending run, was a highlight of that recording. The Esquire Boys also recorded Rock-A-Beatin' Boogie, years before Haley did it himself.

In 1954 he played the famous solo on Rock Around the Clock. He was paid 21 dollars for it. On 17 June of that year he died after a fall down the stairs, ten days after his last session with Haley. Eight months later the song was used in the film Blackboard Jungle and became the first rock and roll recording to top the American chart. Guitarists such as Jimi Hendrix and Pete Townshend cited his solo as an influence. In 2012 the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame finally inducted him, as a member of the Comets.
artiest/danny-cedrone.listen: Listen to the guitar solo in Rock Around the Clock and notice the fast downward run with which it ends. Can you hear how that solo gives the song a blazing finish?

artiest/danny-elfman.text: Danny Elfman (born in 1953) was the singer and songwriter of the rock band Oingo Boingo and taught himself to orchestrate. The director Tim Burton asked him in 1985 for Pee-wee's Big Adventure. Beetlejuice (1988), Batman (1989) and Edward Scissorhands (1990) followed. Elfman writes music that is eerie and playful at once: fast waltzes, children's choirs, celesta and heavy minor-key marches. His Batman theme became a dark superhero march, which set the tone for later superhero films and for the animated series. He also wrote the opening theme of The Simpsons. With Spider-Man (2002) he returned to the superhero genre.
artiest/danny-elfman.listen: Listen for the combination of a heavy, dark march in the low register with a high, fairy-tale-like choir or celesta.

artiest/danny-en-the-juniors.text:
Danny & the Juniors was an American doo-wop and rock and roll group from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The four members were Danny Rapp as lead singer, Frank Maffei as second tenor, Joe Terranova as baritone and Dave White as first tenor. They knew each other from John Bartram High School and began singing together in the mid-1950s, at first as the Juvenaires. The producer John Madara saw their potential and put them in touch with the local disc jockeys Larry Brown and Artie Singer, who had the label Singular Records.

In 1957, as Johnny Madara and The Juvenaires, they recorded a song that Madara and White had written, Do the Bop. Singer played it to his colleague Dick Clark. Clark suggested changing the group's name to the Juniors and giving the song a new title. That is how At the Hop came about, with Danny Rapp on lead vocals. With the line Let's go to the Hop instead of Let's all do the bop, it became a local hit in June 1957. In December 1957 they stepped in at the last moment on American Bandstand and sang it for the whole of America.

ABC Paramount bought the recording and released it in January 1958. At the Hop reached number one on the American pop and rhythm and blues charts in 1958 and number three in England. Rock and Roll Is Here to Stay and Dottie followed as singles. The group also appeared in the 1958 film Let's Rock. In 1960 they signed with Swan Records, Dick Clark's label.
artiest/danny-en-the-juniors.listen: Listen to At the Hop and notice the question-and-answer singing between the lead singer and the backing voices. Can you hear how the group builds the chorus together?

artiest/danny-rampling.text:
Danny Rampling, born in 1961, is an English house DJ who is often named as one of the founders of the British rave and club scene. He began his career in the early 1980s with hip hop, soul and funk in bars and clubs in London. In 1987 he went on holiday to Ibiza with the DJs Paul Oakenfold, Nicky Holloway and Johnny Walker. There they visited the open-air club Amnesia, where they were introduced to the eclectic style of the DJ Alfredo, who among other things played the new house music from the United States.

Back in England, Rampling and his wife at the time, Jenni, tried to recreate the Ibiza feeling with Shoom, England's first Balearic rave club. Shoom ran for three years, beginning in a sports hall in Southwark in London. The club was a springboard for acid house culture and contributed to worldwide dance culture. In 1991 he became the first winner of DJ Magazine's award for best DJ in the world.

In the early 1990s he had the Saturday-night slot Love Groove Dance Party on the pirate station Kiss. From November 1994 he presented that programme on BBC Radio 1, until March 2002. Only Pete Tong's Essential Selection ran longer. He also formed the band The Millionaire Hippies. In the mid-1990s he also played harder, trancey sets, which he himself called Euro. In that period his album A Voyage Into Trance appeared. According to the sources he sold more than a million compilation albums.
artiest/danny-rampling.listen: Listen to a mix by Danny Rampling and notice how the tracks gradually flow into one another. Can you hear where one track ends and the next begins?

artiest/danongan-kalanduyan-and-the-pala.text:
Danongan Kalanduyan was a master of the kulintang, the music of the Maguindanao of the southern Philippines. Anyone who listens to his ensemble hears an age-old gong tradition. Kulintang is the term for a row of small gongs laid horizontally on a rack, which play the melody. They are played with two wooden sticks. Around them sound larger, hanging gongs and drums. The whole falls within the broader gong culture of Southeast Asia, which also includes the gamelan of Java and the piphat of Thailand and neighbouring countries.

The name palabuniyan, in the sources palabunibunyan, means something like an ensemble of loud instruments or making music with kulintang. The ensemble of five or six instruments is also called basalen. The music is orchestral: each instrument has its own rhythmic part, and these layers are stacked neatly on top of one another. The scale is pentatonic. Kulintang music is regarded as a tradition older than the influence of Hinduism, Buddhism, Islam, Christianity and the West. In the Philippines it is seen as the highest form of gong music.

Kalanduyan kept this tradition alive and taught it to a new generation, also outside the Philippines. In this way a musical form that had long remained local reached stages and classrooms in other parts of the world. In the course, his ensemble shows how dance music without piano, guitar or drums can still sound rich.
artiest/danongan-kalanduyan-and-the-pala.listen: Listen to Kapamalong-malong Dance Music I and try to pick apart the different layers: the melody on the row of small gongs and the deeper-sounding gongs and drums around it. Which instrument holds the rhythm together?

artiest/daphne-oram.text:
Daphne Oram was born in 1925 in Devizes, Wiltshire, and died in 2003. She was a British composer and electronic musician, one of the first in Britain to make electronic sound. In 1942 she was offered a place at the Royal College of Music, but she chose a job as a studio engineer at the BBC. There she experimented with tape recorders: she cut, spliced and looped sound, and played it slower, faster and backwards. In this way she was one of the first in the United Kingdom to work in musique concrète.

In the 1950s she pressed the BBC to build electronic music facilities. She was a co-founder of the BBC Radiophonic Workshop. Her uncredited music for the 1961 film The Innocents was one of the first electronic soundtracks. After leaving the BBC in 1959 she founded the Oramics Studios in Kent. There, with the engineer Graham Wrench, she developed Oramics, a technique in which sound is drawn on 35-millimetre film, which photocells convert into sound. She was the first woman to set up her own electronic music studio independently and to design and build an electronic instrument.

In 1971 her book An Individual Note of Music, Sound and Electronics appeared. Still Point, a piece for turntables, double orchestra and microphones, was only performed seventy years later. Her archive is held at Goldsmiths in London. Albums such as Pop Tryouts from 2015 show that her work is still being discovered. Oram is regarded as a pioneer of electronic music.
artiest/daphne-oram.listen: Listen to a piece by Oram, such as Contrasts Essonic, and notice the electronic sounds that do not seem to belong to any familiar instrument. Can you hear how the sound of the apparatus itself becomes the music?

artiest/dario-marianelli.text: Dario Marianelli was born in Pisa and studied in Florence. In 1990 he moved to London. There he took a postgraduate course in composition at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama and then spent three years at the National Film and Television School, from which he graduated in 1997. From 1994 he wrote for film. He often works with the director Joe Wright, including on Pride & Prejudice (2005), Atonement (2007) and Anna Karenina (2012). In Atonement the sound of a manual typewriter is clearly part of the soundtrack. For that score he received an Oscar and a Golden Globe in 2008. Pride & Prejudice and Anna Karenina earned Oscar nominations. He also wrote, among others, V for Vendetta (2006), Jane Eyre (2011) and Darkest Hour (2017).
artiest/dario-marianelli.listen: Notice how in Atonement the tapping of a typewriter joins in as a rhythm with piano and strings, and how Anna Karenina is built on a waltz movement.

artiest/darius-milhaud.text:
Darius Milhaud was born in 1892 in Marseille and grew up in Aix-en-Provence, which he regarded as his true city. He was a French composer, conductor and teacher, a member of Les Six and one of the most prolific composers of the twentieth century. His list of works ends at opus number 443. He began as a violinist and switched to composition. At the conservatoire in Paris he met Arthur Honegger and Germaine Tailleferre. From 1917 to 1919 he was in Brazil as secretary to the poet and ambassador Paul Claudel.

In Brazil he was struck by the popular music of the country. You can hear that in Le Boeuf sur le toit, with melodies by, among others, Ernesto Nazareth, and in Saudades do Brasil, a suite of twelve dances that evoke twelve districts of Rio de Janeiro. In 1922 he heard real jazz for the first time in Harlem, which strongly influenced his music. A year later he completed La création du monde. His music makes much use of polytonality, that is, several keys at once.

Milhaud was also an influential teacher. He taught at Mills College in California and in Paris. His students included Dave Brubeck, Burt Bacharach, Steve Reich, Philip Glass and Karlheinz Stockhausen. Brubeck studied with him because Milhaud incorporated jazz into his work. To Bacharach he said that he should not be afraid of a melody that people can remember and whistle. In this way Milhaud forms a bridge between classical music, jazz and pop.
artiest/darius-milhaud.listen: Listen to La création du monde and notice the saxophone and the bluesy melodies among the orchestra. Can you hear where jazz enters classical music?

artiest/dashboard-confessional.text:
Dashboard Confessional is an American rock band from Boca Raton, Florida, formed in 1999 and led by singer Chris Carrabba. The name comes from the song The Sharp Hint of New Tears on the debut album The Swiss Army Romance. That album appeared in 2000 and began as a solo project of Carrabba's while he was still playing in the band Further Seems Forever. He left that group before their debut was finished, in order to make his second solo album, The Places You Have Come to Fear the Most, and then the EP So Impossible.

By 2002 three other musicians had joined him. After the success of the second album, Carrabba was invited to perform on MTV Unplugged. The live album that came out of it was, for many of the songs, the first time they had been recorded with a full band. In 2002 the video for Screaming Infidelities won the MTV2 Award at the MTV Video Music Awards. In 2003 came A Mark, a Mission, a Brand, a Scar, which reached number two on the American chart and became the commercially most successful album.

In 2004 the band recorded Vindicated for the film Spider-Man 2. Dusk and Summer followed, recorded in 2006 with the producer Daniel Lanois. The Shade of Poison Trees from 2007 returned to the acoustic atmosphere of the first records. The sixth album was called Alter the Ending, from 2009. Later came Covered in the Flood in 2011 and Crooked Shadows in 2018. It remained a band built around one singer and writer, with Carrabba as its constant centre.
artiest/dashboard-confessional.listen: Listen to Screaming Infidelities and notice the acoustic guitar and Carrabba's singing. Does the vocal suit the simplicity of the accompaniment?

artiest/dave-ball.text:
Dave Ball was an English producer and electronic musician, born in 1959 in Chester. He was adopted and grew up in Blackpool. He studied art at Leeds Polytechnic, where he met the singer Marc Almond. In 1978 they began the synth-pop duo Soft Cell together. In that partnership Ball took care of the synthesizers and the music, and Almond the voice and the show.

In 1981 Soft Cell made a version of Tainted Love, a soul song originally sung by Gloria Jones. Ball turned it into a bare, cool electronic version, with a ticking rhythm and a few sharp synthesizer sounds. It became the duo's big hit. Soft Cell lasted until 1984 and reunited a few times later. In 1983 Ball also made a solo album, In Strict Tempo, with, among others, Gavin Friday and Genesis P-Orridge.

After Soft Cell, Ball continued to experiment. He worked with Psychic TV and, with Richard Norris, founded The Grid, a group that made electronic dance music with singles such as Floatation and Swamp Thing. He also produced and remixed for, among others, Kylie Minogue, David Bowie and Erasure. In 2001 he made another album with Almond as Soft Cell. Ball died in October 2025. He is one of the makers who brought the synthesizer from the experimental fringe to the charts.
artiest/dave-ball.listen: Listen to Tainted Love by Soft Cell. Notice how little Dave Ball needs: a ticking rhythm, a few short synthesizer notes and a bass line, above which Marc Almond's voice has all the space it needs.

artiest/dave-brubeck.text: The pianist Dave Brubeck grew up in California and studied composition with the French composer Darius Milhaud. His quartet with the alto saxophonist Paul Desmond played often at universities from the early 1950s and became popular with students as a result. In 1954 Brubeck appeared on the cover of Time. On Time Out (1959) the quartet played in unusual time signatures. Take Five, written by Desmond, is in five beats to the bar; Blue Rondo à la Turk alternates a Turkish rhythm of nine beats with swing. Brubeck had heard that rhythm in the street in Turkey. Take Five became a hit single. Later Brubeck also wrote masses and oratorios.
artiest/dave-brubeck.listen: Count along in Take Five: one-two-three, four-five.

artiest/dave-brubeck-quartet.text:
The Dave Brubeck Quartet was founded in 1951 by the American pianist and composer Dave Brubeck. Brubeck was born in 1920 in Concord, California, and received piano lessons from his mother, who had had a classical training. In the army he had already formed one of the first bands of black and white musicians. The quartet kept its name even when the line-up changed. The most successful line-up played from 1958 to 1967: besides Brubeck, the saxophonist Paul Desmond, the bassist Eugene Wright and the drummer Joe Morello.

In 1958 the quartet made a tour commissioned by the American State Department. That trip inspired the album Time Out (1959). Despite the unusual time signatures, it became the first jazz record to sell more than a million copies. Take Five, written by Desmond in 5/4 time, became the best-selling jazz single ever. Blue Rondo à la Turk, in nine beats, also became a hit. The quartet went on to make four more albums with unusual time signatures, including Time Further Out (1961) with Unsquare Dance.

The group is regarded as one of the most important names in Cool Jazz and West Coast jazz. Brubeck combined jazz with ideas from European classical music, such as fugues and the work of the French composer Darius Milhaud. According to critics, his strength lay in making complicated rhythms and compositions accessible. Brubeck kept making music until his death in 2012.
artiest/dave-brubeck-quartet.listen: Listen to Unsquare Dance (1961). Count along: every bar has seven beats. Notice the handclaps that mark the rhythm and how the bass and piano still move smoothly in that unusual metre.

artiest/dave-davies.text:
Dave Davies is an English guitarist, singer and songwriter, born in 1947 in Muswell Hill in north London. He was the youngest of eight children. The house was full of every kind of music, from his parents' music hall to the jazz and rock 'n' roll of his older sisters. Parties were held in the front room at which the parents sang and played piano. Dave played skiffle at first and then bought an electric guitar. With his older brother Ray and his friend Pete Quaife he jammed in that front room.

In 1963 he started The Kinks with Quaife, and Ray soon joined, becoming the main writer and singer. Three days after Dave turned seventeen, the first single came out. The breakthrough followed in 1964 with You Really Got Me. To make the sound rougher, Dave cut into the speaker of his small Elpico amplifier with a razor blade. This produced one of the first distorted guitar sounds in pop music, with heavy power chords. All Day and All of the Night sounded like that too.

Dave remained in his brother's shadow for the rest of the band's career, and the two had a fierce rivalry. Sometimes he wrote or sang himself, as in Death of a Clown from 1967, which became a hit as a solo single. Later he made solo albums. His distorted riffs had a great influence on hard rock, heavy metal and punk. In 1990 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with The Kinks.
artiest/dave-davies.listen: Listen to You Really Got Me by The Kinks. Notice the rough, crackling sound of the guitar in the two-chord riff: that comes from Dave Davies's slashed speaker.

artiest/dave-fridmann.text:
David Lawrence Fridmann is an American producer and musician. He was the bassist and a co-founder of the band Mercury Rev, in which he played from 1989 to 2001, although he had stopped touring with the group in 1993. From 1990 he co-produced most of the records by Mercury Rev and The Flaming Lips. He gave up his role as a touring member to concentrate on producing other artists.

His best-known productions are The Soft Bulletin by The Flaming Lips from 1999 and their Yoshimi Battles The Pink Robots from 2002, The Woods by Sleater-Kinney from 2005 and Oracular Spectacular by MGMT from 2007. He also worked with Weezer, Sparklehorse, Mogwai, Low, OK Go, Tame Impala, The Delgados and Café Tacuba. In 2007 he received a Grammy for The Flaming Lips' At War With The Mystics, in the category Best Engineered Album. In 2010 three albums he had produced appeared in Rolling Stone's list of the hundred best records of the decade.

MOJO magazine called him the Phil Spector of the alt-rock era in 2001, and included him in its list of a hundred Sonic Visionaries. Fridmann occasionally teaches sound recording at the SUNY Fredonia school of music. In 2017 he became director of the Western New York Alumni Drum and Bugle Corps, where he played the bass drum. He shows how much influence a producer can have on the sound of an era.
artiest/dave-fridmann.listen: Listen to Oracular Spectacular by MGMT and notice the full, layered sound. Can you hear how many different sounds are in the mix at once?
